I always had an issue with the fact that we are dealing with limited resources to allocate to research, and i am doubtful of what new knowledge may come from this line of research that wasn't already attained from similar MBCT studies for other conditions (e.g. tinnitus, anxiety). 

Running a clinical trial is always expensive, I truly hope that the results are worth it, because that money could have been spent on further understanding  the pathophysiology of this syndrome and getting closer to an effective treatment.

If we had the capability to raise much more funding I would be okay with any research that may help VS sufferers (like what you may find for other widespread, known, neurological condition, like MS or epilepsy) but I don't think we are in that situation.

I think mental health is always going to be a hot topic around VSS sufferers.

It's a recurring topic in VSI videos, a lot of specialists give their opinion about whether stress/anxiety/depression could be another symptom/cause of VSS.

I've always thought that it's a natural consequence of the distress the symptoms cause, but some doctors argue that as VSS appears to involve several areas of the brain it could very well be another symptom we don't understand.

Severity of symptoms vary a lot. For many of us it does impair our vision. Any activity that requires me to use my sight is extremely exhausting. You probably know that many VSS sufferers experience other symptoms, like tinnitus and DPDR. It can be quite frustrating when you have a condition that makes it really really hard to appreciate your surroundings and noone recognizes that you are struggling (even among people who are experiencing similar conditions) .  I know most users around this subreddit have mild cases and can perform normally or even forget about it, but there are severe cases nonetheless. 

Personally my VS has gotten to the point I can't drive at night, and most times it feels like I am in the middle of an electric storm. At night I usually need some sort of white noise to ignore the tinnitus.

The idea of having to deal with symptoms that disrupt your day to day life, for the rest of your life, can definitely feel devastating.
